explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 1 says God's Son shows it by sending an angel: “He made it known by sending His angel to His servant John…” So this message came by special delivery, and the courier had wings. I once had an angel show up at my drawer, so I know how a visit like that goes.

Elijah was a prophet of Israel, and a big name, so I see why he's tempting. But this verse never mentions him. It says the revelation reaches John when God sends His angel. Sometimes the answer is simply the one the text gives.

Paul, the apostle, is another name people know, so he's an easy one to grab. But the text never sends him anywhere in this verse. It says the revelation is made known by God's angel, sent to His servant John. No Paul in verse 1, friend.

Not quite, friend. John never calls this his opinion. He says he testifies to everything he saw, and he calls it “the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ.” That's a whole lot bigger than a hot take.

That's right. John doesn't hand this over as his own opinion. He says he testifies to everything he saw, and then he calls it “the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ.” This is a man reporting what he saw, not telling you what he feels like thinking.

explanations.answer: Those who hear and obey it
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The blessing goes to the reader and also to “those who hear and obey what is written in it.” So you can't just nod along and walk away with your hands in your pockets. Hearing and obeying go together, and I'm happy to bake with anybody who signs up for both.

explanations.answer: Those who copy it by hand
explanations.explanation: Copying sounds like holy work, and I'd copy it too if my mustache could hold a pen. But verse 3 never mentions copying. The blessing goes to the one who reads aloud and to those who hear and obey what is written.

explanations.answer: Those who learn it by heart
explanations.explanation: Memorizing is a fine habit, and I'd never talk anyone out of it. But that's not what verse 3 says. It blesses “those who hear and obey what is written in it.” Obeying is the part the text names, friend.

Right on, friend. The grace and peace come from the One who is and was and is to come, from the seven spirits before His throne, and from Jesus Christ. Verse 5 then calls Him “the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.” That's a whole list of titles for one name.

Gabriel, the angel who brought messages to people in Scripture, shows up in other stories. But this greeting never mentions him. John says the grace and peace come from the One who is and was and is to come, from the seven spirits before His throne, and from Jesus Christ.
Moses, Israel's leader, is a giant in the Bible, so I get the pull. But this greeting never names him. The third source in verse 5 is Jesus Christ, the faithful witness.

Yes, friend. Jesus is “the firstborn from the dead,” and that is a big deal. Later in this same chapter He says, “I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever!” (Revelation 1:18). So the Lord's story goes through the grave and comes out the other side.

“Nations” sounds right next to “kings of the earth,” so I see how you got there. But John writes that Jesus is the firstborn from the dead. The kings part is the separate title that comes right before it.
“Heavens” has a nice ring to it, friend. But John doesn't say that. Verse 5 calls Jesus “the firstborn from the dead,” and that word dead matters a lot in this chapter.

That's it, friend. John says Jesus “has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father.” That's a big description for ordinary people, and the text hands it to them. Jesus is the One who made them that, not anything they cooked up themselves.
A city is a fair guess, since Scripture has plenty of those. But verse 6 says Jesus has made His people to be a kingdom. It's a kingdom, with priests to His God and Father.

I can see why an army came to mind, with all the talk of kings. But John doesn't say that. Verse 6 says Jesus “has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father.” No marching orders here, friend.

True, friend. John says, “Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him…” That's not a private showing, and nobody gets left out of the line of sight. Every eye, and I think that includes mine.
Not this time, friend. Verse 7 says, “Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him…” So it's true, and that's every eye. It won't be a quiet event.

Yes. After “every eye will see Him,” John adds “even those who pierced Him.” The text names them on purpose, so they're not left out of the seeing. Then it says “all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him.”
Temple builders are in the Bible, friend, but not in this verse. John says every eye will see Him and then names “those who pierced Him.” That's the group he singles out.

explanations.answer: Those who crossed the Red Sea
explanations.explanation: That's a great Bible moment, but verse 7 doesn't mention it. John says every eye will see Him, “even those who pierced Him.” Different story, friend, and this one is the one on the table.

True. John writes, “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, who is and was and is to come, the Almighty. Notice that it's the Lord God speaking in His own voice, not John. Verse 8 is a different speaker from the verses around it.

Not quite, friend. The line in verse 8 is, “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, who is and was and is to come, the Almighty. So it's true that the Lord God is the One saying it, and John is just passing it along. A new voice, a new speaker.
That's the one, friend. John says he “was on the island of Patmos.” Not a name you forget once you've read it. Patmos is the place where he hears the voice behind him.
Cyprus is an island in the Bible, so I see why it popped up. But John doesn't say he was there. He says he “was on the island of Patmos.”

Crete is a real island in Scripture too, but verse 9 doesn't point there. John says he “was on the island of Patmos.” Islands in the Bible are like cookie cutters: plenty of shapes, and you've got to pick the right one.
True, friend. John says he was on Patmos “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus.” He doesn't give any other reason. I won't add one, either.

Not this time, friend. Verse 9 says John was on Patmos “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus.” So the statement is true, and that's the reason he gives. I won't guess at anything beyond it.
Not quite, friend. The voice says the opposite: “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches…” So John isn't told to keep it to himself. He's told to write it down and send it.

That's right. The loud voice says, “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches…” John is told to send it out, not keep it quiet. And he's told to write it down, so it can travel.

explanations.answer: One like the Son of Man
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. John says, “among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man.” In the Gospels, Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). So this is a lot to take in, and John says it with care.
A mighty angel would be quite a sight, I'll give you that. But John doesn't describe Him that way. He says, “One like the Son of Man.”
The roar in this vision is real, but verse 15 puts it with His voice. His voice is “like the roar of many waters.” The way John describes the One among the lampstands is “One like the Son of Man.”

That's it, friend. John says, “His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.” The sun at full strength is hard to look at, and I think that's the point of the comparison. John chose it to describe what he saw.
The moon is a gentle light, and I like it. But John doesn't use it here. He says His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.
Lightning is bright, and I see why it came to mind. But verse 16 says, “His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.” Sun, not lightning, friend.

explanations.answer: Falls at His feet like a dead man
explanations.explanation: Yes. John says, “When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man.” That's his honest reaction, and I think anyone would struggle to stay standing. Notice the next part, though. He's not left on the floor.

explanations.answer: Covers his face and turns away
explanations.explanation: Turning away makes sense to me, friend, but John doesn't say he did that. He says, “I fell at His feet like a dead man.” And he falls right at the feet of the One he sees.

explanations.answer: Grabs a scroll and starts writing
explanations.explanation: I love the hustle, friend, but not yet. The writing instructions come after, once the One like the Son of Man speaks to him. First John says, “I fell at His feet like a dead man.”
That's right. He puts His right hand on John and says, “Do not be afraid…” Those are the first words John hears from Him. Before any instructions, there's comfort.
That would be a sensible thing to say to a man on the ground. But it's not what the text records. His first words are “Do not be afraid…”

That's a question I could picture asking, friend, but the text gives no question like it. The One like the Son of Man places His right hand on John and says, “Do not be afraid…” A hand first, then words of comfort.

Yes. He says, “I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.” Right before that, He says, “I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever!” So the One who went through death holds its keys. I've had a lot of keys in my life, but never anything like that.
Heaven sounds like a good one to hold keys to, friend. But the text says something different. He says He holds “the keys of Death and of Hades.”
Zion is a name from the Bible, and I get why it came to mind. But it's not in this verse. The keys He holds are “the keys of Death and of Hades.”

explanations.answer: The things that are and that will happen after this
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. He says, “Therefore write down the things you have seen, the things that are, and the things that will happen after this.” That's three sets of things to write: what John has seen, what is, and what will happen after. So he has plenty of scroll work ahead.

explanations.answer: The names of everyone in the seven churches
explanations.explanation: That would be a long scroll, friend. But the text doesn't ask for it. He tells John to write down “the things you have seen, the things that are, and the things that will happen after this.”

explanations.answer: The words the old prophets spoke before him
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, but verse 19 doesn't say it. John is told to write what he has seen, what is, and what will happen after this. It's a command about this vision, friend.
True, friend. He says, “the seven lampstands are the seven churches.” It was a mystery, and then He explains it right away. And remember where He was standing in the vision: among those lampstands.
Not quite, friend. He says, “the seven lampstands are the seven churches.” So the statement is true. The lampstands in the vision stand for the very churches John is told to write to.

explanations.answer: The angels of the seven churches
explanations.explanation: That's right. He says, “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches…” The stars are the ones He held in His right hand. That's the detail from verse 16, explained in verse 20.

explanations.answer: The seven spirits before His throne
explanations.explanation: Those spirits are in the chapter, friend, back in verse 4. But verse 20 says the seven stars are something else. They are “the angels of the seven churches.”

explanations.answer: The seven eyes of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's a phrase I can see you reaching for from somewhere else in the Bible, friend. But it isn't in this chapter. Here, the One like the Son of Man says the seven stars are “the angels of the seven churches.”
